actions.justification: ★ MANDATORY: Patient has hypertension and diabetes type 2 — both major AKI risk factors. Must assess all risk factors including nephrotoxin exposure, volume status, and baseline renal function to guide management.

★ MANDATORY: Patient presents with decreased urine output (oliguria), a cardinal feature of AKI. Continuous urine output monitoring is essential to assess severity, guide fluid management, and track response to treatment.

★ MANDATORY: Serum creatinine is required to confirm AKI diagnosis, stage severity per KDIGO criteria, and establish a baseline for trending. Essential for dosing adjustments and assessing progression.

BMP is critical to assess electrolytes (especially potassium - hyperkalemia risk in AKI), BUN, bicarbonate, and glucose. Patient has DM2 and HTN with AKI - electrolyte derangements and acid-base status must be evaluated urgently.

Patient has edema and decreased urine output with hypertension - distinguishing volume overload (intrinsic/post-renal AKI) from volume depletion (pre-renal AKI) is essential to guide fluid management and avoid harmful fluid administration in oliguric state.

Patient with HTN and DM2 is likely on medications that can worsen AKI (ACEi/ARBs, NSAIDs, metformin, contrast agents). Identifying and discontinuing nephrotoxins is a key early intervention per AKI management guidelines.

Urinalysis with microscopy is essential to identify the cause of AKI - muddy brown casts suggest ATN, WBC casts suggest AIN, RBC casts suggest glomerulonephritis, and proteinuria assessment helps characterize intrinsic renal disease. This is a core KDIGO AKI assessment step not yet completed.

Patient has hypertension and diabetes - likely on ACE inhibitors/ARBs, metformin, NSAIDs, or other nephrotoxic agents. Must identify and discontinue nephrotoxins per AKI management guidelines. Metformin requires dose adjustment or discontinuation in AKI.

Checking baseline eGFR is critical to stage the AKI severity (KDIGO staging) and determine if this is acute-on-chronic kidney disease, which is important for prognosis and management decisions in this diabetic hypertensive patient.
Patient has hypertension (BP 155/95), SpO2 95%, and HR 92 - serial vital sign monitoring is critical to track hemodynamic status and detect deterioration in AKI management.
Urine electrolytes (sodium, creatinine) are needed to calculate FENa and differentiate pre-renal AKI from intrinsic renal causes (ATN), which will guide fluid management decisions.

Patient with creatinine 3.2 and SpO2 95% needs blood gas to evaluate for metabolic acidosis (common in AKI), assess acid-base status, and guide urgent management including potential need for renal replacement therapy.

Volume status assessment is critical in AKI to differentiate pre-renal (volume depletion) from intrinsic causes. Patient has decreased urine output and swelling which could indicate either fluid overload or third-spacing. This directly guides fluid management.

FENa (Fractional Excretion of Sodium) is a key diagnostic test in AKI to differentiate pre-renal azotemia (FENa <1%) from intrinsic renal disease such as ATN (FENa >2%). With creatinine of 3.2 and oliguria, this is essential to guide management.

Urinalysis with microscopy is essential to identify the cause of AKI - muddy brown casts suggest ATN, RBC casts suggest glomerulonephritis, WBC casts suggest AIN/pyelonephritis. Patient has proteinuria pending and this will help characterize the renal injury.

Creatinine 3.2 indicates severe AKI with high risk of hyperkalemia. Potassium monitoring is critical to detect life-threatening electrolyte abnormalities. Per universal safety guidelines, severe renal impairment requires close electrolyte monitoring.

Renal ultrasound is essential to rule out post-renal obstruction (hydronephrosis) as a cause of AKI. Patient has decreased urine output and swelling, making obstructive uropathy an important differential to exclude before attributing AKI solely to pre-renal or intrinsic causes.

Patient has hypertension and diabetes type 2 as comorbidities — both major risk factors for AKI and CKD. Reviewing risk factors helps characterize the etiology and guides management decisions including medication adjustments per renal function.

Patient has SpO2 95% and peripheral swelling suggesting possible pulmonary edema/fluid overload. Chest X-ray is essential to assess cardiac size and pulmonary congestion before any fluid management decisions.
Renal ultrasound to evaluate for post-renal obstruction (hydronephrosis) as a reversible cause of AKI. This is a distinct action from any previously completed renal imaging order.

Contrast-induced nephropathy is an important reversible cause of AKI. Reviewing recent contrast exposure helps identify etiology and guides avoidance of further nephrotoxic contrast agents per KDIGO guidelines.
Patient has creatinine 3.2 with AKI - nephrotoxic agents (NSAIDs, contrast, aminoglycosides) must be discontinued immediately per AKI management guidelines to prevent further renal injury.
CBC not yet ordered - needed to evaluate for anemia (common in AKI/CKD), infection/inflammatory cause of AKI, and thrombocytopenia that may indicate TTP/HUS or other intrinsic renal cause.

Cystatin C provides a more accurate GFR estimate than creatinine alone, especially important in this diabetic patient to better characterize severity of renal impairment and guide medication dose adjustments.

Patient has AKI with creatinine 3.2. All nephrotoxic agents (NSAIDs, contrast, aminoglycosides) must be discontinued to prevent further renal injury. This is a distinct action_id from the already-completed 'discontinue_nephrotoxins'.

Patient has decreased urine output and swelling (edema) suggesting possible fluid overload. Fluid status optimization is critical - avoid excessive fluids in oliguric AKI while ensuring adequate perfusion. BP is elevated at 155/95 suggesting volume overload rather than pre-renal state.
Serial creatinine trending is essential to monitor AKI progression or recovery. The baseline creatinine is 3.2; repeat measurement will help assess trajectory and guide management decisions.

Patient has AKI with creatinine 3.2, hypertension, diabetes, and SpO2 95% - nephrology consultation is warranted for expert management of moderate-to-severe AKI, guidance on renal dose adjustments, and evaluation for potential renal replacement therapy if condition worsens.
AKI can be associated with coagulopathy; coagulation studies are important to assess bleeding risk and guide management in this patient with creatinine 3.2 and pending labs.
Patient has elevated RR of 20, SpO2 95%, and AKI - lactate helps assess for tissue hypoperfusion or lactic acidosis contributing to or resulting from renal dysfunction.

Patient has AKI with creatinine 3.2, hypertension (BP 155/95), diabetes, and SpO2 95% — nephrology consultation is warranted to guide further management, especially given the severity of renal impairment and comorbidities. Note: consult_nephrology was previously done but request_consultation is a distinct available action for additional specialist input (e.g., endocrinology for diabetes management in AKI context).

Patient has decreased urine output and swelling; careful IV hydration may be appropriate if pre-renal component is contributing to AKI. Must be administered cautiously given oliguria and risk of fluid overload, titrated to urine output targets.

Urinalysis was ordered but urine culture is needed to rule out infectious/obstructive etiology contributing to AKI, especially important in a diabetic patient who is at higher risk for urinary tract infections causing renal impairment.

Patient has AKI with creatinine 3.2, elevated BP, and decreased urine output. Volume status optimization with cautious crystalloid administration may help maintain renal perfusion in pre-renal or mixed AKI component. Already completed optimize_fluid_status assessment; now executing fluid administration based on hydration assessment findings. Avoid excessive fluids given oliguric state - administer carefully with monitoring.

Patient has AKI with creatinine 3.2 and severe renal impairment. If contrast imaging is needed, calculating the contrast volume limit is essential to minimize further nephrotoxicity per KDIGO AKI guidelines.
If contrast must be used in this patient with AKI (creatinine 3.2), low-osmolar contrast should be used to reduce risk of contrast-induced nephropathy per standard nephroprotective protocols.
Patient has creatinine of 3.2 with AKI. Formally staging the AKI per KDIGO criteria (Stage 1/2/3) guides management intensity, RRT planning, and nephrology communication.
Calculate eGFR based on current creatinine (3.2) to quantify degree of renal impairment, guide drug dose adjustments, and assess need for RRT per KDIGO guidelines.

Universal safety guideline mandates dose adjustment for renally cleared drugs in severe renal impairment. Patient has creatinine 3.2 and comorbidities (HTN, DM2) requiring multiple medications that may need renal dosing.

Patient has AKI with creatinine 3.2 and decreased urine output. Severe AKI commonly causes hyperkalemia, which can cause life-threatening arrhythmias. ECG is indicated to assess for peaked T-waves, widened QRS, or other signs of hyperkalemia.

With creatinine 3.2, oliguria, and significant AKI, renal replacement therapy may be needed. Assessment criteria include refractory hyperkalemia, metabolic acidosis, uremic symptoms, or fluid overload unresponsive to diuretics.

Given the severity of AKI (creatinine 3.2, decreased urine output, volume overload with swelling), proactive RRT planning including vascular access consideration should be initiated in case the patient deteriorates or meets RRT indications.
Patient has creatinine of 3.2 with AKI - formal evaluation of RRT indications (refractory hyperkalemia, acidosis, uremia, fluid overload) is warranted given severity of renal impairment.
With creatinine 3.2 and established AKI with hypertension and diabetes comorbidities, nephrology input is needed for ongoing management guidance if not already formally consulted via this pathway.

Patient with diabetes and hypertension presenting with AKI is at high risk for progression to CKD; early assessment and documentation of CKD risk factors guides long-term management and follow-up planning.

Despite extensive workup, formal identification and documentation of AKI etiology (pre-renal vs intrinsic vs post-renal) is needed to guide ongoing management, especially with creatinine at 3.2 and pending labs.
Patient has diabetes type 2 and AKI with creatinine 3.2 - metformin is contraindicated in significant renal impairment due to risk of lactic acidosis and should be held immediately.
NSAIDs are nephrotoxic and contraindicated in AKI. Patient has hypertension and diabetes increasing risk - these must be held to prevent further renal injury.
